newsitem.title: FRANCE: CGIP to decide on Cap Gemini within month.
newsitem.headline: CGIP to decide on Cap Gemini within month.

text.p: French holding company CGIP said on Thursday it would decide within a month whether to exercise its option to buy the 24.4 percent stake in French computer systems firm Cap Gemini put up for sale by Daimler-Benz.

Compagnie Generale d'Industrie et de Participations (CGIP), which holds 20 percent of Cap Gemini, has right of first refusal on the stake through an agreement with Daimler-Benz InterServices (Debis), a spokeswoman said.
CGIP said in a statement that the German industrial giant's decision to dispose of its stake in Cap Gemini was "positive" and "put an end to a long period of uncertainty".
"CGIP will decide its position on whether to exercise its right of refusal contained in agreements with Debis within the month," it said.
CGIP said in January that its shareholding in Cap Gemini was "totally satisfactory for us" and that the company was firmly on the road to recovery after several difficult years.

Cap Gemini also praised the German group's decision, saying it "lifted the uncertainty which had weighed for several months" on the group. But its shares fell, trading 3.18 percent lower at 334.0 at mid-morning.

There had been expectations that Daimler-Benz might make an offer for CGIP's 20 percent stake and CGIP had been pressing the German company to make up its mind on the future of its involvement in the company.
But Daimler-Benz said on Wednesday it would sell the stake which it had held for six years, dousing speculation that it planned a takeover of the French company.
It said it would sell the stake in "the medium term", using a convertible bond which would generate proceeds of more than one billion marks.
It said it was making the move because of differing strategic focuses.
Earlier on Thursday, Cap Gemini announced that its profits should be in line with shareholders' expectations.
It gave no further details but the market consensus expectation is for a net profit of around 500 million francs in 1997 after a 282 million profit in 1996.
